title: Serialize and Deserialize a Binary Tree
prompt: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize that string back into the exact same tree structure. Serialization is the process of converting the in-memory tree to a string (or byte stream) so it can be stored or transmitted; deserialization reconstructs the original tree from that string. The tree is a general binary tree — values may repeat and are not ordered. You define the format; serialize(deserialize(t)) must reproduce t.
blurb: You own the wire format — the crux is encoding null children so structure is unambiguous, then reconstructing in the same traversal order.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Recognizes it's a general (unordered, possibly-duplicate-value) tree, so structure must be captured explicitly; clarifies value domain and null representation.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Picks a traversal (preorder DFS or level-order BFS) and commits to encoding nulls as explicit markers so the structure is recoverable.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Deserialize consumes tokens in the SAME order serialize produced them; null markers reconstruct missing children exactly; round-trips arbitrary shapes.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(n) time and O(n) space for both directions; notes recursion/queue depth and output size are O(n).

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean token stream (delimiter + null sentinel), a shared index/iterator for deserialize, no fragile string parsing.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Empty tree (null root), single node, skewed/degenerate tree, duplicate values, negative values, values containing the delimiter.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Round-trips a skewed tree and an empty tree, and confirms duplicate values don't corrupt reconstruction.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Clearly states the format contract (delimiter, null sentinel, traversal order) before coding, so both halves agree.

constraints: -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000 (values may repeat; tree is not a BST)
Format is your choice, but serialize then deserialize must reproduce the identical tree
Must handle the empty tree (root == null)

examples.input: root = [1,2,3,null,null,4,5] (1 with left=2, right=3; 3 has children 4 and 5)
examples.output: serialize -> "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#" (preorder with '#' for null); deserialize rebuilds the identical tree
examples.explanation: Preorder visits 1, then left subtree (2 with two null children), then right subtree (3, then 4 with nulls, then 5 with nulls). '#' marks every absent child so structure is unambiguous.

examples.output: "#" (a single null marker); deserialize returns null
examples.explanation: The empty tree must round-trip too.

test_cases.expected: round-trips to a single node with val 7 ("7,#,#")
round-trips; duplicates don't confuse reconstruction because position, not value, drives structure
round-trips; parser must handle the minus sign, not split it as a delimiter

reference.optimal_time: O(n) to serialize and O(n) to deserialize (each node visited once)
reference.optimal_space: O(n) for the output string plus O(h) recursion stack (or O(n) queue for BFS)

approaches.name: naive: preorder values only (no null markers)
approaches.idea: Emit just the node values in preorder. This is ambiguous for a general tree — many distinct trees produce the same value sequence — so it cannot be deserialized uniquely. (It works ONLY for a BST, where a preorder sequence plus the ordering invariant is enough.)
approaches.note: Rejected for general trees: structure is lost.

approaches.name: optimal A: preorder DFS with null sentinels
approaches.idea: Serialize with a recursive preorder that emits each node's value, then recurses left, then right; emit a sentinel (e.g. '#') for null children. Deserialize reads tokens left-to-right with a shared cursor: read a token; if '#', return null; else create a node, then recursively build left, then right. The null markers make the structure unambiguous.

approaches.name: optimal B: level-order BFS (LeetCode-style)
approaches.idea: Serialize by BFS, emitting values level by level with a sentinel for each null child of a real node. Deserialize with a queue: the first token is the root; then consume pairs of tokens as the left/right children of dequeued nodes, enqueuing non-null children. Produces the familiar bracket-array format.

approaches.name: length-prefixed / typed encoding (robustness)
approaches.idea: For a compact binary format, write a null bit per child and length-prefix each value, avoiding delimiter-collision issues entirely. More work but robust to arbitrary value content.

follow_ups: Reconstruct a BST from preorder ONLY (no null markers) using value bounds — O(n) — and explain why the general tree can't do this.
Serialize an N-ary tree: encode each node's child count, or use null/'end-of-children' markers.
Make the format compact: bit-per-null-child + fixed-width or varint values; compare size vs. the CSV-with-'#' format.
Make it delimiter-safe: what if values are arbitrary strings that may contain the comma/'#'? (length-prefixing or escaping).
Deserialize iteratively instead of recursively to avoid stack overflow on a skewed 10^4-deep tree.
reference.reference_solution: Format contract: comma-separated tokens, '#' for null, preorder. serialize(root): use a helper that appends to a list: if node is null, append '#'; else append str(node.val), then recurse(node.left), then recurse(node.right). Join with ','. serialize(null) -> '#'. deserialize(data): split on ',' into tokens; keep a shared index (closure/iterator). build(): read tokens[i]; i++; if token == '#' return null; node = TreeNode(int(token)); node.left = build(); node.right = build(); return node. The invariant is that build() consumes exactly the tokens serialize emitted for that subtree, in the same preorder, so left is fully consumed before right begins. This is why duplicate values are fine — position in the stream, not value, determines structure. For an iterative deserialize (avoiding deep recursion), the BFS/queue variant is cleaner: read root, push to queue; while tokens remain, dequeue a parent and assign its next two tokens as left/right children, enqueuing any non-null child.
pitfalls: Omitting null markers — structure becomes ambiguous for general trees (only works for BSTs).
Deserialize reading tokens in a different order than serialize wrote them (e.g. right before left).
Using a value that can appear in the data as the delimiter/sentinel — pick a sentinel outside the value domain or length-prefix.
Mishandling the empty tree (null root) as a special case.
Recursive deserialize blowing the stack on a 10^4-deep skewed tree — mention the iterative option.

interviewer_notes: This tests format design as much as coding. The single most important early question to see them ask (or to prompt): 'is this a BST or a general tree?' — because a general tree needs explicit null encoding. If they propose preorder-values-only, hand them two different trees that produce the same value sequence and let them discover the ambiguity themselves rather than telling them. Stay silent through the recursion; the classic bug is deserialize consuming tokens in a different order than serialize wrote — surface it by asking them to trace [1,2,3,null,null,4,5]. Confirm they handle the empty tree. Escalate strong candidates to: reconstruct a BST from preorder alone (bounds trick, O(n)), then a compact binary/varint format, and finally an iterative deserialize to survive a 10^4-deep skewed tree.
